subject: Automotive & EVs
title: The Interstate Highway System
description: A 60-second lesson on The Interstate Highway System.

hook.text: In the 1950s, President Eisenhower signed the largest public works project in US history.

buildup.text: He had seen Germany's Autobahn during the war and wanted America to have a connected highway network.

discovery.text: The 1956 Highway Act funded 41,000 miles of interstate roads. It cost $25 billion—over $500B today.

twist.text: Highways cut through cities and displaced entire neighborhoods, often poor and minority communities.

climax.text: But they also made cross-country driving possible and created the trucking industry we rely on today.

punchline.text: Highways connected America but divided many cities.

details.summary: President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act in 1956, creating the Interstate Highway System that connected American cities with over 48,000 miles of high-speed roads.
details.whyItMatters: The Interstate System was the largest public works project in history, enabling long-distance car travel, spurring suburban growth, and reshaping the American economy around the automobile.
takeaways: The system spans over 48,000 miles across all 50 states
It was partly inspired by Germany's Autobahn network
Construction took over 35 years and cost hundreds of billions

faq.question: Why did Eisenhower push for the Interstate system?
faq.answer: His experience moving troops across poor US roads in 1919, combined with admiration for Germany's Autobahn and Cold War defense needs for rapid military transport, motivated the initiative.

faq.question: Did the Interstate system have negative effects?
faq.answer: It devastated many urban neighborhoods, particularly minority communities, through highway construction that bisected thriving districts. It also accelerated suburban sprawl and urban decline.
